nameStory: The long-headed poppy gets its name from its distinctive elongated seed capsules that look like tiny elongated heads or clubs. Unlike the round, bulbous seed pods of most poppies, this species develops narrow, oblong capsules that are much longer than they are wide. The alternate name 'blindeyes' likely refers to the small pores that open at the top of the mature seed capsule, resembling tiny unseeing eyes.
description: Long-headed poppy is a delicate annual wildflower that stands about 1-3 feet tall with a slender, branching stem. It produces bright red or orange-red flowers with four papery petals that have a silky, crinkled texture like tissue paper. The plant has deeply divided, feathery leaves that give it a lacy appearance. As a non-native species from Europe, it's quite rare in New England, preferring disturbed sandy soils.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: The seed capsule is distinctively long and narrow - like a skinny club or elongated teardrop - much longer than it is wide, distinguishing it from other poppies with round pods

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Four bright red to orange-red petals with a silky, crinkled texture that feels like delicate tissue paper; flowers are about 1-2 inches across with dark stamens in the center

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Deeply cut, feathery leaves that are finely divided into narrow segments, giving the plant a lacy, delicate appearance; leaves feel soft and slightly fuzzy

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Slender annual plant growing 1-3 feet tall with branching stems that feel somewhat brittle; the whole plant has a wispy, delicate appearance

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Flowers nod downward in bud, then face upward when open; petals drop easily when touched, leaving the distinctive long seed capsule behind

habitat: Look for long-headed poppy in sandy, disturbed soils without lime, such as old fields, roadsides, construction sites, and waste areas. It strongly prefers sandy or gravelly soils and avoids rich, heavy, or alkaline soils. Being extremely rare in New England with only 4 recorded observations, it's most likely to turn up as a chance introduction near ports, railroads, or other areas with soil disturbance.

seasonality.spring: Seeds germinate in early spring, and young plants develop their characteristic feathery foliage. Look for the distinctive deeply-cut leaves emerging from disturbed sandy soil.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming occurs from late spring through mid-summer, with bright red flowers opening in succession. The diagnostic long, narrow seed capsules begin forming as flowers fade.
seasonality.fall: Mature seed capsules split open at the top to release tiny seeds. The annual plant begins to die back, turning brown and brittle.
seasonality.winter: Dead stems and empty seed capsules may persist through winter in protected spots, but the annual plant is gone until seeds germinate the following spring.

funFact: Long-headed poppy seeds are so tiny that a single plant can produce over 20,000 seeds, and these seeds can remain dormant in the soil for decades, suddenly sprouting when construction or other disturbance brings them back to the surface and light!
confusionNotes: Most likely to be confused with the more common corn poppy (Papaver rhoeas), but corn poppy has round, bulbous seed capsules while long-headed poppy has distinctively elongated, narrow capsules. Remember: 'long-headed' = long capsules, corn poppy = compact round capsules.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called a poppy and sharing the same genus as the opium poppy, long-headed poppy contains no significant amounts of narcotic compounds and is not used medicinally. Like other members of the poppy family, all parts of the plant contain a milky sap, but it's not the same alkaloid-rich latex found in opium poppies.
compareHints: Long-headed poppy is most easily distinguished from corn poppy (Papaver rhoeas) by its elongated seed capsules versus corn poppy's round ones. Compared to opium poppy, long-headed poppy is much smaller and more delicate, with finely divided leaves rather than opium poppy's broader, less-divided foliage. Oriental poppy is a perennial garden plant with much larger flowers and different leaf structure entirely.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Common poppy is much smaller and more delicate than Oriental poppy, with thinner petals and smaller flowers.
Unlike the common red poppy with its bright scarlet petals and hairy stems, opium poppies have that distinctive blue-green, waxy appearance and much larger flowers in various colors.

Unlike its annual cousins like corn poppy (which has smaller, more delicate flowers and stays visible all season), Oriental poppy is a robust perennial with much larger flowers and hairy, substantial foliage.
Unlike the bright red Common Poppy or the large, vivid Oriental Poppy, Atlas Poppy has distinctly pale orange flowers that are much more subtle.
